paragraphs: What I have said so far applies to all nations. The remark I am about to make, however, is particular to the Americans and to democratic peoples. I have already observed that in democracies the lawyers and the judges form the only aristocratic body able to check the excesses of the people. This aristocracy holds no physical power, but it exercises a conservative influence over people’s minds, and the richest source of its authority is the institution of the civil jury. In criminal cases, society is armed against a single individual, and the jury tends to see the judge as a passive instrument of social power and to distrust his advice. Criminal cases also rest entirely on evidence of facts that common sense can readily weigh, and on that ground the judge and the jury are equals. Civil cases are different. There the judge appears as a disinterested arbiter between the conflicting passions of the parties. The jurors look up to him with confidence and listen to him with respect, because here their intelligence is wholly under the direction of his learning. It is the judge who sums up the various arguments that have worn out their memory, and who guides them through the winding course of the proceedings. He directs their attention to the exact question of fact they are called on to decide, and he puts the answer to the question of law into their mouths. His influence over their verdict is almost unlimited.

Suppose I am asked why I am so little moved by the arguments drawn from the ignorance of jurors in civil cases. I answer that in these proceedings, whenever the question to be decided is more than a question of fact, the jury has only the appearance of a judicial body. The jury confirms the decision of the judge: the jurors do so by the authority of the society they represent, and the judge by that of reason and of law. *h

In England and in America, judges have an influence on criminal trials that French judges have never had. The reason for this difference is easy to find. English and American judges establish their authority in civil cases, and only afterward transfer it to courts of another kind, where they did not acquire it. In some cases, often the most important ones, American judges have the right to decide alone. *i On these occasions they happen to stand in the position that French judges habitually occupy. But they hold far more power than the French judges do. They are still surrounded by the memory of the jury, and their judgment carries almost as much authority as the voice of the whole community, which that institution represents. Their influence extends beyond the courts. In the recreations of private life and in the turmoil of public business, in public places and in the legislative assemblies, the American judge is constantly surrounded by men who are used to regarding his intelligence as superior to their own. And after he has exercised his power in deciding cases, he continues to shape the habits of thought and the characters of the people who took part in his judgment.
i [ The Federal judges decide on their own authority almost all the questions most important to the country.]

The jury, then, which seems to limit the rights of the judges, in reality strengthens their power. In no country are judges so powerful as where the people share their privileges. It is above all through the jury in civil cases that American judges imbue every class of society with the spirit of their profession. Thus the jury, which is the most energetic means of making the people rule, is also the most effective means of teaching the people to rule well.
